newsitem.title: USA: U.S. homebuilding surges in November.
newsitem.headline: U.S. homebuilding surges in November.

text.p: Construction starts on new homes jumped at the sharpest rate in more than a year last month, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, putting builders on track for their best year since 1988.
Total starts increased 9.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.514 million in November, the biggest monthly increase since an 11.5 percent surge 16 months earlier in July 1995.
The brisk gain in November starts followed back-to-back drops of 5.1 percent in October starts and a 4.7 percent fall in September.
Analysts said moderately lower mortgage rates in November fostered the bounce-back but were surprised at the vigour of the pickup in building activity.

"Basically, this appears to be a case of builders catching up to demand right now because our purchase applications are very high," said economist David Lereah of the Mortgage Bankers Association, referring to would-be homeowners' bids for mortgages.
"We should see good, solid buying activity for the next month or so," Lereah added, but rates have moved up slightly from November and may put a damper on future sales.

The strength in November building was broad-based, with starts on single-family homes climbing 7.6 percent to a rate of 1.164 million a year and apartment starts up steeply by 15.1 percent to 350,000 a year.
The report of surging construction came shortly before Federal Reserve policy makers met to consider interest-rate strategy, though analysts did not expect it to play a role in the Fed's decision.
The pace of homebuilding in the first two months of the final quarter has slowed moderately from the third-quarter average and is forecast to continue doing so next year.

"We expect the market to subside somewhat in 1997," said David Seiders, an economist with the National Association of Home Builders. He forecast starts on new single-famnily homes and apartments at about 1.35 million next year.
But for 1996, Seiders said, starts appear likely to come in around 1.475 million, up 9 percent from 1995 and the strongest year since 1988 when builders broke ground on 1.488 million new homes.
"It's a healthy industry," Lereah said. "Inventories are relatively low, interest rates are favourable, the economy is still growing and people are still buying big-ticket items."
In addition to the improvement in construction, applications for new building permits picked up in November after three consecutive monthly drops, rising 3.9 percent to 1.415 million.

The National Association of Home Builders said on Monday that its index of market activity gained slightly in December, reversing a downward trend that began in June and virtually ensuring the industry will finish the year on a strong note.
"The recent decline in interest rates has apparently improved builders' perception of the marketplace," said assocation President Randy Smith, a builder in Walnut Creek, Calif.
Mortgage rates remain relatively low by historical standards and even declined in November.
The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., or Freddie Mac, said rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.58 percent in November, down from 7.92 percent in October.
Total housing starts during November were 3.8 percent higher than a year earlier, when new homes were being started at an annual rate of 1.458 million.

The only region in which starts declined last month was the Northeast, where they fell 2.2 percent to 131,000 a year. Starts were unchanged from October in the West at a rate of 364,000 during November.

But in the South -- the biggest regional market -- November starts rose briskly by 12 percent to 337,000 a year. In the Midwest, they gained even more strongly by 20.8 percent to an annual rate of 337,000.
